cards.front: What do the two axes of an energy diagram show?
cards.back: The **vertical axis** shows energy, and the **horizontal axis** shows reaction progress. Reaction progress is not elapsed time.
cards.hint: Ask yourself whether the horizontal axis has a time scale.

cards.front: What is the activation energy on an energy diagram?
cards.back: The **energy difference** between the reactant level and the peak of the reaction pathway. The peak is the transition state.
cards.hint: Measure it vertically, from reactants up to the peak.

cards.front: How do you calculate the reaction enthalpy, $\Delta H$, from an enthalpy diagram?
cards.back: $\Delta H$ = **product enthalpy minus reactant enthalpy**. Products below reactants give a negative value, so the reaction is exothermic.
cards.hint: Subtract the starting level from the ending level.

cards.back: The **highest-energy** arrangement along a reaction pathway. It is short-lived and is not an isolable product.
cards.hint: It sits at the peak of the curve.

cards.front: Does a wider curve on an energy diagram mean a slower reaction?
cards.back: No. **Reaction progress** has no time scale, so width does not show speed. Barrier height is what matters for rate.
cards.hint: Horizontal distances do not show time.

cards.front: Does a high peak mean a reaction is endothermic?
cards.back: No. Only the **starting and ending levels** decide whether $\Delta H$ is positive or negative. The peak sets the activation energy.
cards.hint: Compare the reactant and product levels only.

cards.front: What are the steps to read both barriers and $\Delta H$ from an energy diagram?
cards.back: Read all three levels. Forward barrier = peak minus reactants. Reverse barrier = peak minus products. $\Delta H$ = products minus reactants, keeping the sign.
cards.hint: Read every level before you subtract.

cards.front: Reactants are at 40 kJ/mol, the peak at 110 kJ/mol, and products at 10 kJ/mol. What is $\Delta H$?
cards.back: $\Delta H = 10-40 = -30\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. The reaction is **exothermic** because products lie below reactants.
cards.hint: Products minus reactants, and keep the negative sign.

cards.front: Using the same diagram (reactants 40, peak 110, products 10 kJ/mol), what is the reverse activation energy?
cards.back: $110-10 = 100\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. It is measured from the **product level** up to the peak.
cards.hint: Start from the product level, not the reactant level.

cards.front: Where should the activation energy arrow start and end?
cards.back: It should run from the **reactant level** up to the peak. Do not measure it from the bottom of the axis.
cards.hint: Think about where the barrier actually begins.

cards.front: What does a catalyst change on an energy diagram?
cards.back: A catalyst provides a **lower-barrier pathway**, so the activation energy falls. The reactant and product energy levels stay the same.
cards.hint: Which levels move, and which stay put?

cards.front: How does an endothermic reaction look on an enthalpy diagram?
cards.back: The **products lie above** the reactants, so $\Delta H$ is positive.
cards.hint: Compare the ending level with the starting level.
